In Apple's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (fiscal year ended September 27, 2025), the legal-proceedings and government-investigation disclosures (Item 3, and the related risk factor discussion) date the following developments to specific days or months of calendar 2025:

**April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act (two actions, same day)** (Item 3, "Digital Markets Act Investigations")
- **Article 5(4) Investigation:** The European Commission fined Apple €500 million and issued a cease-and-desist order requiring it to remove technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. - **Article 6(4) Investigation:** The Commission issued preliminary findings in its separate investigation into whether Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces may violate the DMA. **April 30, 2025 — Epic Games litigation** (Item 3, "Epic Games")
The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Injunction and enjoined Apple from (i) imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app, (ii) restricting, conditioning, limiting, or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to outside purchases, or (iii) otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app. The court also denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. Apple's request to stay the decision pending appeal was denied.

**October 2025 — Epic Games appeal** (Item 3)
The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals agreed to hear Apple's appeal on an expedited basis, with oral arguments heard in October 2025.

**September 2, 2025 — Google antitrust remedies** (Item 1A risk factors, regarding a company with which Apple has commercial relationships)

## 2025 strike by IAM District 837 employees

- **Employee count:** Approximately **3,200 employees** at Boeing's St. Louis area sites (stated in the Human Capital section, the union risk factor, and the MD&A overview).
- **Duration:** The strike lasted **101 days** (Human Capital section, page 4, and risk factor, page 11).
- **Calendar dates:** The work stoppage was **initiated on August 4, 2025**, and ended on **November 13, 2025**, when IAM District 837 voted to ratify a new contract (MD&A Overview, page 26).
- **What it refers to:** The strike **disrupted Boeing's St. Louis operations** and impacted defense programs including **F/A-18, F-15, T-7A Red Hawk, MQ-25 and Weapons**. Both the Human Capital and risk-factor sections note it occurred despite Boeing having reached a tentative agreement with union leadership, which had recommended members ratify the proposed contract. For context, IAM agreements overall cover 25% of Boeing's workforce.

## Current collective bargaining agreement with IAM District 837

- Per the principal collective bargaining agreements table in the Human Capital section (page 4), Boeing's major agreement with **IAM District 837** is located in **Missouri** and has an **expiration date of July 2030**.
- This is the successor contract ratified on November 13, 2025 that ended the 101-day strike — the filing does not give separate terms beyond the location and expiration date in that table.

In short: ~3,200 St. Louis-area employees, 101 days, August 4 – November 13, 2025, disrupting F/A-18, F-15, T-7A, MQ-25 and Weapons programs — and the resulting contract with District 837 runs until July 2030.

I've reviewed the 10-K body (financial statements, notes, and risk factors — exhibits excluded). Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K gives three dollar amounts for dividends on the 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock:

**1. $345 million — maximum annual cash dividend requirement** (Item 1A, Risk Factors, p. 17)
Boeing states it "expect[s] to require up to **$345 million** of cash per year for the payment of dividends on the outstanding shares of our 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock... through the mandatory conversion date of October 15, 2027." This represents the full-year cash cost of the cumulative dividend on the 5,750,000 outstanding preferred shares (payable when, as and if declared, in cash, common stock, or a combination).

**2. $58 million — dividends accumulated during 2024** (Consolidated Statements of Operations, p. 54; Note 4 – Earnings Per Share, p. 73)
Line item: "Mandatory convertible preferred stock dividends accumulated during the period — **$58**" (millions) for 2024. This represents the preferred dividends that accumulated from the October 31, 2024 issuance through year-end, deducted from net loss attributable to Boeing shareholders ($11,817M) to arrive at net loss attributable to Boeing common shareholders ($11,875M).

**3. $72 million — dividends declared in December 2024** (Note 19 – Shareholders' Equity, p. 106; Consolidated Statements of Equity, p. 58)
"In December 2024, dividends of **$72** were declared to holders of record as of January 1, 2025, representing **$12.50 per share**, and were paid in cash on January 15, 2025." It represents the first quarterly cash dividend declared on the new preferred stock (paid after year-end, so no cash dividend outflow appears in 2024 financing activities).

In short: **$345 million** (annual cash requirement going forward), **$58 million** (accumulated in 2024 for EPS purposes), and **$72 million** (declared December 2024, paid January 15, 2025).

Pfizer's 2021 Form 10-K gives these figures for costs of separating the former Upjohn Business (separated November 16, 2020 and combined with Mylan to form Viatris):

- Location: Item 7 MD&A, "Our Business and Strategy" (Form 10-K page 26)
- Stated as: "We expect to incur costs of approximately $700 million in connection with separating Upjohn, of which, approximately 75% has been incurred since inception and through December 31, 2021."

## Effect of the January 1, 2023 adoption of the TDR accounting guidance

JPMorgan Chase adopted the FASB's "Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings (TDRs)" guidance under the **modified retrospective method on January 1, 2023**, and its 2023 Form 10-K gives the following dollar amounts:

### Effect on the allowance for credit losses / allowance for loan losses

**Net decrease of $587 million** to the Firm's allowance for credit losses. This is the cumulative-effect adjustment recorded on January 1, 2023, and it measures the reduction in the allowance for loan losses that resulted from (a) eliminating the requirement to measure the allowance for TDRs using a discounted cash flow (DCF) methodology and (b) the Firm's election to apply its non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance approach to loans modified for troubled borrowers for all portfolios — except collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual risk-rated loans, which remained on the DCF/asset-specific approach (its adoption did not change the collateral-dependent allowance approach). Stated another way, the $587 million is the difference between the allowances previously carried for TDRs under the DCF method and the allowances recognized under the portfolio-based approach.

The 10-K breaks this $587 million cumulative effect down by loan portfolio segment in the allowance for loan losses rollforward (Note 13 and the MD&A "Allowance for Credit Losses" table):

| Loan portfolio segment | Cumulative effect (in millions) |
|---|---|
| Consumer, excluding credit card | $(489) |
| Credit card | $(100) |
| Wholesale | $2 |
| **Total allowance for loan losses** | **$(587)** |

(The lending-related commitments allowance had no cumulative-effect impact, and the MD&A separately notes the total allowance for credit losses "reflected a reduction of $587 million as a result of the adoption.") No business-segment-level (CCB/CIB/CB/AWM) dollar amounts are disclosed — the breakdown is only by loan portfolio segment.

### Effect on retained earnings

**Increase of $446 million, after-tax**, to retained earnings. This measures the after-tax income-equivalent of the $587 million allowance reduction recorded as a cumulative-effect adjustment to retained earnings at the January 1, 2023 adoption date; the 10-K states it was "predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card."

(For completeness: the Consolidated statement of changes in stockholders' equity shows a "Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" of $449 million in 2023, which combines the $446 million TDR adoption effect with the immaterial retained-earnings effect of the separately adopted fair value hedging – portfolio layer method guidance.)

I found the answer in the MD&A discussion of Berkshire Hathaway Energy (pages K-43 to K-44 of the filing). Here's what the 2024 Form 10-K says:

## Why BHE is evaluated on after-tax earnings

The filing explains the after-tax basis with two related reasons:

**1. Income taxes are built into the regulated rates BHE's customers pay.** The filing states:

> "The rates BHE's regulated businesses charge customers for energy and services are largely based on the costs of business operations, **including income taxes** and a return on capital, and are subject to regulatory approval. To the extent such costs are not allowed in the approved rates, operating results will be adversely affected."

In other words, income taxes are treated as a recoverable cost of doing business in BHE's regulated utility rate-making. Because taxes flow directly through customer rates, pre-tax earnings are a less meaningful gauge of BHE's performance than they are for businesses whose prices are set by competitive markets.

**2. It reflects how the businesses are actually managed.** The filing states explicitly:

> "The discussion of BHE's operating results that follows is based on after-tax earnings, **reflecting how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated**."

## Supporting context from the same discussion

- BHE's summary table shows a **negative effective income tax rate** — an income tax *benefit* of $1.87 billion in 2024 (effective rate of (81.6)%), driven by "significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation." This makes the tax line a substantial driver of BHE's economics, not a mere deduction, further reinforcing the after-tax view.
- By contrast, the Manufacturing, Service and Retailing businesses are presented on a **pre-tax earnings** basis (with taxes and noncontrolling interests deducted as a single line), since income taxes are not recovered through customer rates for those businesses.

In short: because BHE's regulated rates are set to recover operating costs including income taxes plus a return on capital, and because large tax credits (like wind production tax credits) are integral to results, the filing evaluates BHE on after-tax earnings consistent with how management runs the energy businesses.
